_comment: What a sector makes, consumes and throws off.
WHY MATERIALS ARE A NODE KIND. The layer could already say that a technology addresses
a constraint and that a project deploys the technology. It could not say what any of it
is made of. That gap is not academic: the prices that decide whether a route pays —
the allowance price, scrap, hydrogen, electricity — are prices OF MATERIALS, and with
nowhere to hang them they were sitting on measures and technologies as if they belonged
to the instrument rather than to the thing being bought. Materials are also the only
object that joins two sectors honestly: blast-furnace slag leaving steel and arriving in
cement is one node with an edge on each side, not a sentence on two pages.
THE FIVE TYPES. `by_product` and `waste_stream` are kept apart deliberately — a
by-product has a buyer, a waste stream has to be paid to take away — because a page that
grouped them would assert a market that may not exist. Captured CO2 is a waste stream
today and would move to by_product the day somebody is reliably paid for it.
EDGES LIVE ON THE MATERIAL. Every edge incident to a material is recorded here, the same
arrangement bottlenecks.json uses, so there is one file to read and one place to gate:
produced_by    sector: | project:   -> this material comes out of it
consumed_by    sector: | technology: -> this material goes into it
substitutes    another material id   -> this one can stand in for that one
required_by    technology:           -> the technology cannot run without it, and does
not consume it (an energy carrier, a catalyst).
Empty on cement: everything here is consumed.
Each edge carries `since` and `evidence`, as every edge in this repository does, and
`volume` where a sourced parameter states one. `volume` names a parameter id rather than
restating a number, so a material cannot carry a figure that is not in parameters.json
with the sentence it was read from.
WHAT IS MISSING. Slag and fly ash — the clinker substitute the brief asks for third —
are not here, and the reason is the rule rather than the effort: no source stating the
substitution has been read, and an edge without evidence is the one thing this layer
does not ship. See GAPS.md, which names the document that would fill it.
crma_annex_i  WHETHER THE MATERIAL IS A STRATEGIC RAW MATERIAL under Annex I of
the Critical Raw Materials Act, brief 5 §2. Null where it is not,
which is both materials on the platform today: clinker and a
captured CO2 stream are neither of them raw materials the Union
has listed. Where it is, the value is the Annex I entry as the
annex words it plus the source it was read from, and the sector
page renders it as a tag on the material — a fact about the
material, never a judgement about the sector that handles it.
The field is REQUIRED and explicit rather than absent-means-no:
an unlisted material and a material nobody has checked are the
same object otherwise, which is the mistake the scope attribute
in ROADMAP.md is written about.

materials.name: Clinker
materials.description: The calcined intermediate that carries almost all of cement's process CO2. A tonne of cement is a tonne of clinker plus additions, which is why every carbon instrument that reaches this sector is written per tonne of clinker rather than per tonne of the product sold.

produced_by.volume_note: EU clinker output is unsourced and is the gap blocking every sector total on this page — see GAPS.md, 'EU clinker output'.

evidence.quote: Grey cement clinker | 0,689 | 0,656
evidence.note: The ETS free-allocation benchmark is set per tonne of grey cement clinker produced, which is the Commission stating what this sector's benchmarked output is.

materials.name: Captured CO2
materials.description: What a capture plant produces and cannot sell. It is abated only once it is stored, so every tonne recorded here is a tonne owed to a transport and storage chain built by other parties on other timetables.

evidence.quote: Brevik CCS will capture around 400,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year, representing 50% of the plant's emissions.
capturing 700,000 tonnes of CO₂ annually from 2029.
will have a capture capacity of about 800,000 t CO₂ per year

produced_by.volume_note: The release states the capture rate on the treated stream and no tonnage for the pilot unit, so this edge carries no sourced volume.

evidence.quote: capture the CO2 present in blast furnace gases emitted during steel production at ArcelorMittal's Dunkirk site
evidence.note: The first non-cement producer of this material. One node with an edge on each side is what the material kind exists for, and it is also why the CO2 transport and storage constraint is now a constraint on two sectors rather than one.

materials.name: Steel scrap
materials.description: Recovered steel, remelted in an electric furnace with no ironmaking step and therefore none of ironmaking's CO2. It is the only decarbonisation input this sector already has at scale, and the only one whose supply is fixed by what Europe scrapped twenty years ago rather than by what anyone decides to build.

evidence.quote: Just over 40% of EU steel is produced via the EAF production route.
evidence.note: A claim about the industry rather than about a countable set of installations: two fifths of European output already comes off this route.

materials.name: Directly reduced iron
materials.description: Iron reduced in the solid state rather than smelted, and the thing every European conversion is being built to make. It carries the sector's decarbonisation in one object: the same material is near-zero or not depending only on whether the gas that reduced it was hydrogen.

evidence.quote: The 100% hydrogen-capable DR plant with two melters has a production capacity of 2.5 million metric tons of directly reduced iron per year
Around 100 tonnes have been made so far.

produced_by.volume_note: The release states the stage's crude steel capacity, not the direct reduction unit's own output, so no sourced volume attaches to this edge.

evidence.quote: 1.9 million tonnes of crude steel per year
The 100% hydrogen-capable DR plant with two melters has a production capacity of 2.5 million metric tons of directly reduced iron per year
evidence.note: The melters are on the same site as the direct reduction unit: this sector makes the material and feeds it straight back in, which is why the same node is both an output and an input here. The two appearances rest on different edges.

materials.name: Granulated blast furnace slag
materials.description: What runs off a blast furnace and is quenched into a glassy sand that sets like cement. It is the one material that joins these two industries in the wrong direction: it leaves steel as a by-product and arrives in cement as a substitute for clinker, so every furnace steel converts away from also takes away part of cement's answer.

evidence.quote: Depending on the individual blast furnace capacity yearly 150-800 thousand t of GBS will vanish together with each substituted blast furnace.
evidence.note: The volume is stated as what is LOST per furnace converted, which is the only figure the source gives and the one that matters: the quantity is falling by construction as this sector decarbonises.

evidence.quote: For decades blast furnace slag has been used mainly as a cementitious material (if it is glassy due to a quenching process for the liquid slag)
evidence.note: The substitution edge only. No consumed_by edge into cement is recorded here, because that is a claim about the cement sector's inputs and belongs with the cement dataset; see data/transition/GAPS.md.

materials.name: Hydrogen
materials.description: The reducing gas that makes direct reduction near-zero rather than merely lower. Nothing in European steel runs on it at scale yet, which is why it is recorded against the route that needs it rather than against the industry: an edge from the sector would assert a consumption that has not started.

evidence.quote: SSAB, LKAB and Vattenfall have now produced the world's first hydrogen-reduced sponge iron at a pilot scale.
evidence.note: A technology edge, which by the membership rule confers no sector: this material is read on its own page rather than in the steel sector's inputs, and that is correct until a site consumes it.

materials.description: The metal both lithium chemistries are named after, and the one the Union lists in a battery grade of its own. It is recorded against the routes that use it rather than against the industry, because no site here is sourced as consuming a stated tonnage of it.

source.title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1252 (Critical Raw Materials Act), Annex I — strategic raw materials

materials.description: The anode side of the same dependence, and the half of a cell this dataset can say least about. The Union lists a battery grade of it; no source read here states where a European line buys it, and the anode is outside this dataset's perimeter as a works.

evidence.quote: graphite — battery grade
evidence.note: The listing is the evidence: the Union names a battery grade of graphite as strategic, which is a claim that this material goes into cells. No source read here states a European line's supply of it.

materials.name: Sodium
materials.description: The material that is on this platform for what it removes rather than for what it adds. It is in no annex of the Critical Raw Materials Act, which is the whole of its interest: a chemistry built on it answers a supply constraint by leaving the listed metal out.

evidence.quote: Sodium in place of lithium in the cell.
evidence.note: No European site makes these cells, so this edge is to the route and not to a works — the same membership rule hydrogen is held to.

evidence.quote: it removes lithium from the bill of materials entirely, which is the reason it is on this list: the constraint it answers is supply rather than emissions
evidence.note: A substitution at a stated cost: the description says the energy density is lower than either lithium chemistry, so this edge is about supply and not about performance.
